BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: An upper-level low pressure system will weaken as it moves onshore Sunday and Monday, sending embedded shortwave troughs through the area. The greatest precipitation chances will be limited to the higher terrain.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Cool and unsettled pattern will continue periods of valley rain and accumulating mountain snow today through Friday.
- Snowflakes with little to no accumulation possible throughout the Snake Plain Friday morning.
- Return of unsettled patterns with precipitation chances Sunday through late next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Much of the short term's weather will be influenced a strong closed low pressure system moving eastward over the area. Moisture wrapping up into the center of the low pressure won't require much orographic influence to produce precipitation as soundings follow a moist adiabat to the top of the troposphere. Moisture will remain plentiful through Friday morning, before tapering off as the system rejoins the primary flow. This time frame will see continued valley rain and wintry mix, and mountain snow. Snow levels this afternoon through early tonight remain around 4.5 kft MSL in SE OR and 5.5-6 kft MSL in SW ID. Friday morning snow levels drop sharply down to 2.5 - 3.5 kft MSL, again higher in Idaho. This will be low enough for mixed precipitation in the Snake Plain, with a good chance for many locations to see snowflakes even with surface temperatures above freezing. With a persistent cold bias in the model consensus, forecast temperatures during this cold window were made warmer. However, this still leaves a 40% chance for precipitation to fall as snow if precip does fall in the Treasure Valley. By the time things taper off, about 1-3 inches of snow will have fallen in Central Idaho, 2-6 inches in SE Oregon high terrain, and 0.1-0.2 inches of rainfall in low elevations.

Cooler temperatures and gusty northwest winds expected Friday as the area comes under the drier backend of the trough. A brief upper ridge will build into the region Saturday, keeping the area dry but barely warmer. Temperatures will stay near normal through the weekend and colder than previous days. Late Saturday night the next system begins to approach.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: An upper-level low pressure system will weaken as it moves onshore Sunday and Monday, sending embedded shortwave troughs through the area. The greatest precipitation chances will be limited to the higher terrain. The west-central ID mountains will see a 40-60% chance of snow showers Sunday with lower chances Monday, with similar chances across the southwest Idaho highlands. Snow levels will hover near valley floors most of Sunday through Tuesday. The Treasure Valley will see around a 10-20% chance of a rain/snow mix in the early morning hours Sunday and Monday. A brief upper-level ridge will build in Tuesday, returning drier conditions and a slight warming trend. Late Tuesday through Thursday, the overall pattern favors unsettled conditions, however there is considerable uncertainty over the trajectory of another strong Pacific upper- level low affecting the region.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Cooler temperatures will continue across the forecast area through this forecast. Low temperatures Sunday through the middle of next week will be in the teens to 20s.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Next storm system arrives Friday, bringing chances for light mountain snow through Saturday.
- Gusty winds and elevated fire weather conditions on Friday across most of the Front Range foothills and plains.
- Cooler pattern emerges this weekend into next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Tomorrow, an 80kt 500mb jet will move over the area ahead of the approaching shortwave. At 700mb, models have winds around 35kts to 55kts. Conditions do not look favorable for mountain wave amplification in our area due to the flow being more southwesterly and a few other factors. However, we are expecting strong winds to be forced/mixed down to the surface in the late morning through the afternoon. Wind gusts across the plains will be around 30 to 50mph in the afternoon. The one exception will be the northern I-25 corridor and portions of the northern plains, which tend to remain more sheltered from the strong winds in southwest flow. In the higher elevations, wind gusts will near 50 to 65mph in the late morning. A front will approach our northern counties late Friday afternoon, turning winds more towards the west/northwest in our northern counties. This will allow for stronger winds to finally make their way into the northern I-25 corridor and northern plains, with gusts around 25mph to 40mph. There will be elevated fire weather conditions Friday afternoon due to the winds, but relative humidities are forecast to remain above critical thresholds. The front will move through the area overnight, bringing cooler temperatures for Saturday.

The approaching shortwave, weak orographics, and weak surface convergence could be enough to trigger a few showers in the higher terrain and plains overnight Friday into the late morning Saturday. Moisture will be rather limited, so snow accumulations will remain on the low end. With the exception of the Park Range, which should see slightly higher amounts, snow accumulations will generally be a few hundredths to about 3 inches in the higher terrain. Chances for at least a trace of snow in the metro remains on the low end (~20% chance or less). Temperatures will likely support at least a rain/snow mix if not all snow Saturday morning across the plains, it's just the lack of moisture and lack of a strong forcing that's inhibiting snow chances across the plains.

Cooler temperatures will continue across the forecast area through this forecast. Low temperatures Sunday through the middle of next week will be in the teens to 20s. Our next system will approach Colorado on Monday, with a shortwave moving through late Monday into Tuesday. The timing and positioning of the shortwave varies between models, lowering our confidence in precip chances with this system. Right now, we expect light snow showers in the mountains with a medium chance (30% to 50%) that snow showers make it onto the plains. If we do end up with some snow over the plains, accumulations will be light and impacts are not anticipated. The active pattern is expected to continue into later next week, but models continue to swing back and forth with the potential impacts and confidence in any one model solution is very low at this time.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Thursday...Another shortwave trough aloft moves across Wyoming with scattered coverage of orographic snow showers for our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges, dry elsewhere. Similar temperatures when compared to Wednesday with 700 mb temperatures nearly the same.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Critical Fire Weather conditions are ongoing across portions of Carbon and Albany Counties through the afternoon hours.
- Locally heavy snow showers will return to Carbon County and portions of Albany/Converse Counties Thursday night into Friday morning.
- Another round of strong, gusty winds is expected Friday into Friday night.
- Expect chillier temperatures this weekend into early next week with a few additional chances for light, spotty snow showers.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Critically dry conditions have been ongoing across the CWA this morning and afternoon as dew points have tanked into the teens to single digits and even some negative values across portions of southeastern Wyoming. With lingering breezy winds accompanying this critically dry environment, a Red Flag Warning was necessary for portions of I-80 from Arlington through the Laramie Valley and into the southern Laramie Range foothills. While winds have finally started to subside a little bit, gusts exceeding 25 mph will continue to be possible through the next few hours.

Tonight into tomorrow the cold front associated with a deep Pacific trough will move across the region, bringing cooler temperatures and our next chances at precipitation. Best QPF remains to the south and east of our CWA, and the best forcing will be due to orographic features, but snow showers across our western counties will be possible tomorrow. Overall amounts are still outside of thresholds needed for advisory products or higher, but the peaks of the Sierra-Madre range could near 5 inches when all is said and done by Saturday morning. And any snow showers that do occur will have meager instability, so we can't rule out the possibility of a snow squall occurring. Gusty winds likely to accompany this system as pressure gradients begin to strengthen, but in-house guidance has only around a 40% probability for the wind prone locations to reach high wind criteria (58+ mph), and looking at pressure gradients they're just below what we would like to see to solidify stronger winds. Therefore, continued to abstain from issuing any wind related products. Look for chilly temperatures as we move into Saturday morning, with sub freezing lows across the entirety of the region and wind chills in the teens to single digits.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Saturday...Shortwave trough energy moves past the forecast area, with most locations remaining dry. 700 mb temperatures near -7 Celsius will yield high temperatures in the lower 30s to lower 40s.
Sunday...Dry west southwest flow aloft prevails. The atmosphere looks too dry at low and mid levels for any precipitation.

Monday...The flow aloft backs to southwest in advance of the next shortwave trough aloft approaching from Utah. Scattered coverage of orographic snows on tap for our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges. 700 mb temperatures near -5 Celsius will yield high temperatures in the 30s.
Tuesday...The next open trough aloft moves over the forecast area, with a chance of rain and snow early in the day, then drying noted in the afternoon.
Wednesday...Shortwave ridging develops across Wyoming, keeping it dry. A warming trend develops with downslope warming and rising 700 mb temperatures.

Thursday...Another shortwave trough aloft moves across Wyoming with scattered coverage of orographic snow showers for our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges, dry elsewhere. Similar temperatures when compared to Wednesday with 700 mb temperatures nearly the same.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Unsettled weather will return to the region during Thanksgiving week, though specific timing and track details remain uncertain. Even so, a series of disturbances propagating through the area will likely bring minor travel impacts to the mountains.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Measurable snowfall is expected Thursday night into Saturday for the mountains, with some high valleys also seeing light accumulations.
- Temperatures will trend downward for the weekend, with most desert valleys seeing their first freezing temperatures of the year.
- Fast moving storms are possible through much of Thanksgiving week. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: An upstream cyclone continues moving onshore into the Pacific Northwest today, with its associated moisture streaming into the Intermountain West this afternoon on strong southerly flow aloft. This moisture plume will reach our western CWA by late afternoon as the nose of the jet pushes into the region, aligning along an axis from southeast Utah to the northern mountains by Thursday nightfall. Current high-resolution guidance indicates weak instability accompanying this system, which will likely result in streaky, banded precipitation. Due to this convective nature, confidence remains low regarding widespread or prolonged impacts.

That said, there remains a roughly 70% probability of 4 to 6 inches of snow across the higher elevations of the Elk, West Elk, Flat Tops, and Park ranges. The eastern Uintas will see a slightly higher ceiling, with a ~70% chance of 4 to 8 inches due to a longer duration of snowfall compared to surrounding areas. Across the open travel corridors, expected accumulations are lower, and hazardous travel impacts remain uncertain. Meanwhile, persistent moist southerly flow across the southern mountains will keep light flurries lingering over the highest peaks, though the deepest moisture will exit the region before the main axis of instability shifts east Friday afternoon.

Wind will be an additional concern during this forecast period. As the jet noses into the region, gusty winds will develop today and persist into Friday, with gusts reaching up to 45 mph in spots, particularly across higher elevations. Combined with falling or fresh snow, these gusts could produce localized areas of blowing snow and reduced visibility.

By Saturday, a trailing lobe of energy will rotate through the Great Basin toward the Four Corners. Although deep moisture will be largely scoured out by this point, dynamic forcing and increasing snow ratios could still trigger a brief burst of heavier snowfall rates over the southern mountains. Because this wave will be relatively fast-moving, accumulations over the southern mountains should generally remain around 3 to 6 inches. Temperatures will also trend colder behind this system this weekend, bringing single-digit lows to higher elevations.

Unsettled weather will return to the region during Thanksgiving week, though specific timing and track details remain uncertain. Even so, a series of disturbances propagating through the area will likely bring minor travel impacts to the mountains. Continue to monitor the latest forecasts as model consensus improves on the timing of these waves. Daily highs and lows will also trend roughly 5 degrees below seasonal normals.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: The system on Thanksgiving looks less dicey than the ones before it, but scattered precipitation is still possible, and warrants watching given the high volume of travel that will be occuring on Thanksgiving.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Strong winds expected over the southern Sangres and gap flow areas along I-25, starting tonight and lasting into Friday.
- Windy and warm across the area on Friday.
- Quick-moving system comes in Friday Night, bringing a few inches of snow to the mountains with lower chances for a wintry mix for parts of the plains.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A broad upper trough and intensifying low pressure system continues to move towards our region from the west. Through the rest of today and into tomorrow, winds will be picking up across SE Colorado, though the area will remain dry through at least tonight.

Starting overnight, south winds will pick up over the southern plains, mountains, and parts of the San Luis Valley, turning more southwesterly as the upper jet max moves overhead and enhances vertical mixing. Winds will peak during the mid-late morning on Friday, with gusts over the peaks of the mountains in excess of 65 mph. Some areas just lee of the terrain may be shielded from the strongest winds, but we can still expect some gap flow onto I-25 during this timeframe as well, peaking around midday at 40 mph or so.

Our main problem areas with the incoming wind will be the gap flow areas along southern I-25, mainly Huerfano County, and the southern Sangre de Cristos, which show just enough of a mountaintop inversion to suggest the chance for some downsloping-enhanced winds. As such, have upgraded to a High Wind Warning for these areas, valid 11pm tonight through 5pm Friday. The northern Sangres, according to the latest data, do not have the same inversion, so while winds over the peaks will be strong as well, the kinetically-driven mixing regime there won't support consistent highlight criteria. The same can also be said for Pikes Peak and areas just lee of it, though both areas will have to be closely monitored for any changes in the thermal profile that could support stronger gusts.

Elsewhere, winds will be gusty but below highlight criteria on Friday. High temperatures will remain in the 40s-50s over the valleys, increasing over the plains into the mid-high 60s thanks to downsloping.
By late afternoon, the southwest flow aloft will carry moisture into the Continental Divide, with isolated to scattered snow showers moving over the high peaks that will continue into Saturday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A strong jet will have setup by Friday night. It will be the strongest to our South, but it will generate southwesterly winds. We are expecting the Sangre De Cristo mountains to receive a hit of accumulating snowfall between 2 and 4 inches Sunday morning into the afternoon. Then, portions of the I-25 corridor, particularly near the Palmer Divide, could receive some snowflakes Saturday afternoon into evening. Cold air is in ample supply aloft, but a shallow moist layer and limited forcing will mean significant accumulations are not likely, but a brief dusting on non-heated surfaces can't be ruled out.
After our Saturday system, we anticipate cooler temperatures and lighter winds to be the pattern across the region, on account of the cold front passing and a high pressure behind it.

Looking at the next work week, the forecast begins to diverge. Two more precipitation events are in the cards, one Monday night into Tuesday, and one on Thanksgiving. For the Mon-Tue system, the GFS is projecting a more impactful event for our area than the ECMWF. If the former verifies, the I-25 corridor could again see a dusting, especially further north, and our Central Mountains could orographically lift a modest hit of snow Tuesday morning for Lake and Chaffee Counties. That said, looking at the ensembles and probabilistic forecasting, I am leaning towards the ECMWF solution for Tuesday, where all we'd get are some overcast conditions.

The system on Thanksgiving looks less dicey than the ones before it, but scattered precipitation is still possible, and warrants watching given the high volume of travel that will be occuring on Thanksgiving.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: With no blocking ridge developing off the Pacific coast, this break in the action will be short lived, with increasing confidence that an active pattern will persist for much of the upcoming week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A Pacific Northwest storm system will bring periods of snow to Utah's mountains through early Saturday, increasingly focused over northern Utah as time goes on. Significant snow accumulations will bring travel difficulties to high elevations routes. Snow levels will drop to northern Utah valley floors Friday night, bringing a chance of accumulating snow.
- Freezing temperatures are increasing in probability for the Virgin River corridor near Zion National Park Saturday and Sunday mornings.

- Dry conditions are expected over the weekend before a weaker system impacts primarily southern Utah Monday into Tuesday. An active pattern is expected to continue for the remainder of the upcoming week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A broad trough currently is currently centered over the Pacific Northwest, with the associated frontal boundary over eastern Nevada this morning. In moisture and instability on the leading edge of the system, precipitation has already begun over the western half of Utah, with snow levels in the 5500-6500 foot range. Thus, mountain snow is already accumulating. This system will come through Utah and southwest Wyoming in pieces through early Saturday.

Light and steady precipitation is expected to continue during the day today, with a burst of heavier valley rain/mountain snow tonight into early Friday as the frontal boundary crosses the area. Behind the front, precip will become primarily focused over northern Utah where the best cold pool instability will remain. As the main trough tracks across the area, temperatures and thus snow levels will steadily lower during the day Friday, bringing snow levels down to northern Utah valley floors late Friday into early Saturday, bringing the potential for accumulating snow. Limiting factor on those accumulations will be the duration of precipitation after snow levels lower sufficiently and that rates will be generally lower during this time.

Overall, guidance has been trending upward with snowfall totals over the last several runs, particularly over northern Utah. With two feet of snow now in the forecast for portions of the Wasatch including the Upper Cottonwoods, have upgraded both the northern and southern Wasatch mountain zones to a Winter Storm Warning given anticipated impacts with other headlines unchanged at this time.

Behind the exit trough, confidence is high that high pressure will track across Utah and southwest Wyoming Saturday into Sunday, bringing dry conditions. With the clearing and unseasonably cool airmass, freezing temperatures will be in play for lower elevation portions of southern Utah, with the best chance in the Virgin River corridor of Zion National Park. This remains more likely Friday night/Saturday morning than on Sunday morning. Temperatures in the vicinity of St. George are also expected to get close to freezing, though there is a relatively low chance of temperatures moving to or below freezing overnight during that period.

With no blocking ridge developing off the Pacific coast, this break in the action will be short lived, with increasing confidence that an active pattern will persist for much of the upcoming week. The next storm system is expected to move through Monday into Tuesday. Latest guidance is leaning toward a solution that is noticeably weaker than the last couple of systems, bringing minor impacts to primarily southern Utah. Beyond that, there is the potential for a stronger system to move through for the middle to latter part of next week.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: You can trigger avalanches large enough to bury you at upper elevations. You can trigger these slides from the side or bottom of a slope. Steer clear of steep slopes where you encounter wind-stiffened snow or see shooting cracks as you travel. Look for and avoid drifted snow below ridges and on the sides of gullies.
Below treeline conditions are generally safe.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe and lack sufficient coverage for an avalanche. At high elevations, steer clear of isolated patches of firm, drifted snow below ridges or in steep gullies.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Dylan Craaybeek
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe from avalanches. You might be able to trigger a small avalanche where you encounter stiff, wind-drifted snow on the lee sides of ridgelines or above treeline terrain where blowing snow accumulates.
